summary.text: The Reformation was a major 16th-century movement in Western Christianity that challenged the pope and the authority of the Catholic Church's leaders.
It is usually dated from 1517, when Martin Luther published the Ninety-five Theses, and it marked the beginning of Protestantism.
The Reformers argued that people are justified by faith in Jesus Christ alone, and the printing press let religious works spread quickly in local languages.

facts.label: Printing's role
facts.value: Spread religious works rapidly in local languages

facts.label: Wars that followed
facts.value: European wars of religion killed seven to seventeen million

facts.label: Reformed tradition
facts.value: Zwingli and Calvin helped develop it

facts.label: Modern wording
facts.value: Historians often use the plural, since parallel movements drove it

items.prompt: A preacher in 1530 says charity cannot add anything to what makes a person right with God. Which camp is he in?

options.label: Catholic, which linked faith and charitable acts together
Reformers, who rooted it in faith in Christ alone
Catholic, which held that charitable acts replace faith
Reformers, who held that faith and charity count equally

items.explain: The Reformers held that justification rests on faith in Jesus Christ alone, not on faith plus charitable acts as in the Catholic view.

items.prompt: In 1520 a reformer wants ordinary townspeople across Europe to read his arguments quickly and in their own tongue. What helps most?

options.label: Council decrees read aloud in every parish
Hand-copied manuscripts passed between scholars
Gutenberg's press, spreading religious works locally
Sermons given only inside the largest cathedrals

items.explain: Gutenberg's printing press made it possible to spread religious materials rapidly in the local vernacular.

items.prompt: The Council of Trent clarified disputed Catholic positions and abuses that reformers had criticised. What was it part of?

options.label: The Radical Reformation, a return to early practices
The Magisterial Reformation, mainstream Protestantism
Lutheranism, the movement that began in Saxony
The Counter-Reformation, the Catholic response

items.explain: The Counter-Reformation was the Catholic response to the Reformation, and the Council of Trent was central to it.

items.prompt: A group in the 1500s wants to abandon church structures and return to how the earliest Christians lived. Who fits best?

options.label: Anabaptists, a radical branch of the Reformation
Lutherans, who led the mainstream Reformation
Anglicans, who followed a Reformed framework
Calvinists, who developed the Reformed tradition

items.explain: Radical Reformers such as the Anabaptists sought to return to the practices of early Christianity, unlike the mainstream Magisterial Reformers.

items.prompt: Why do many historians now write about the Reformations in the plural?

options.label: Because it happened across several separate centuries
Because it grew from parallel movements, not one uniform event
Because only Catholic and Protestant churches took part
Because Luther's church split into exactly two branches

items.explain: Since the late 20th century historians stress that the Reformation was not uniform and coherent but the result of parallel movements.

items.prompt: A teacher wants one event to mark the day the Reformation began, using the most common choice. Which event?

options.label: Luther posting his theses at Wittenberg's castle church
The Peace of Augsburg being accepted by the princes
Zwingli preaching against abuses in the Church
The outbreak of the Thirty Years' War in Bohemia

items.explain: The most commonly used starting date is 31 October 1517, when Luther allegedly nailed up his Ninety-five Theses in Wittenberg. The other events are end-date or minority start-date choices.
